content: When obtaining informed consent from participants under the age of 18, it may sometimes be inappropriate or potentially harmful to involve their parents. In such cases, investigators can request a waiver for parental informed consent. For example, this could apply to surveys involving drug users under 18 who live and work away from their parents. Such a waiver must be submitted to and approved by the governing Research Ethics Committee (REC) for each protocol. While it is generally advisable to provide participants with a copy of their consent form, caution should be exercised when dealing with stigmatized populations, such as men who have sex with men (MSM) or people who inject drugs (PWID). Instead, investigators can provide minimal information, such as their contact details and those of the appropriate REC. Protecting participants' privacy and confidentiality is critical in surveys. Privacy refers to an individual’s ability to control access to themselves or their personal information, which can vary depending on the context. For instance, protecting a child’s privacy may require the presence of a parent or guardian, while protecting a young person’s privacy might involve withholding survey participation details from their parents or guardians. Investigators must ensure the safety and security of survey participants, particularly when working with vulnerable or marginalized populations. Survey sites and hours should be chosen to ensure participants feel safe from harassment by the public or law enforcement. Participants should not be visible to outsiders during the survey, and their responses should not be audible to others. Investigators should consult with the target population and service providers to select appropriate survey sites. For populations engaged in illegal activities, guidance from the target population may be necessary to determine whether to inform local law enforcement to minimize risks of harassment or raids. Surveys should only collect and record information that is necessary and relevant to the study’s objectives. For example, personal hobbies or home addresses are unrelated to HIV or sexually transmitted infection (STI) risk behaviors and should not be included. Confidentiality refers to the protection of private information provided by participants, which should only be disclosed as outlined during the informed consent process. Survey staff should sign confidentiality agreements, and data dissemination must ensure that no individual participant or group can be identified. Personal identifying information, such as names, phone numbers, addresses, or social security numbers, should not be recorded in surveys. Surveys should be conducted anonymously, using unique survey codes that do not include personal identifiers. Data security measures must be in place to protect participants’ privacy and the confidentiality of their information. Paper-based data should be stored in locked rooms or cabinets, while electronic data should be password-protected. Any data shared outside the survey team must be anonymized. Participants may be reimbursed for travel costs, time spent, lost wages, or other expenses incurred during the survey. Free medical care may also be provided. However, the reimbursement should not be so substantial that it coerces participation, especially in resource-limited settings. The type and amount of reimbursement should be determined in consultation with the survey population and stakeholders and approved by the governing REC. Test results that are clinically meaningful and beneficial to participants’ health should be returned. Procedures for returning results must be clearly described during informed consent. Confidentiality is best maintained through anonymous, linked specimen testing. For participants who wish to know their HIV or STI test results, processes should be in place for easy return of results and post-test counseling. Rapid testing, where feasible, allows results to be returned during the initial survey contact. In other cases, participants may return to the survey site to obtain their results, with measures in place to verify their identity. Adverse events, such as breaches of confidentiality, arrest, or errors in post-test counseling, must be promptly reported to the governing REC. Serious adverse events, such as life-threatening incidents or those resulting in hospitalization or death, require immediate attention. Unexpected adverse events, not anticipated in the protocol, must also be reported. Protocol deviations, whether or not they pose risks to participants, should be reported to the REC and may necessitate protocol amendments. Any changes to approved survey materials or procedures must be submitted to the REC for review and approval. Investigators and survey staff interacting with participants must receive training in human subjects research ethics. This training typically covers ethical principles, REC responsibilities, participant privacy and confidentiality, informed consent procedures, and reporting of adverse events and protocol deviations. Examples of relevant courses include the Collaborative Institutional Training Initiative (CITI) course, the NIH’s Protecting Human Research Participants course, and others. Special considerations are required when conducting surveys among incarcerated populations, who are particularly vulnerable. These populations often have lower socioeconomic status, education levels, and access to health and legal services, as well as higher rates of infectious diseases, chronic illnesses, and mental health issues. Maintaining privacy and confidentiality in prison settings is challenging due to close monitoring by prison officials and other inmates. Prisoners may fear repercussions for participating or not participating in surveys, including threats, abuse, or punishment. Survey methods must be designed to uphold participants’ rights to privacy, confidentiality, and autonomy. Incarcerated individuals may feel coerced into participating due to pressure from prison authorities or the desire to access health services offered as part of the survey. Investigators should minimize discrepancies in health services provided to participants and nonparticipants. For example, confidential HIV and STI testing services could be made available to all inmates during the survey period, but only data from selected participants would be recorded and reported. Web-based surveys present unique ethical challenges. Investigators must consider that internet protocol (IP) addresses may be regarded as personal identifiers by Institutional Review Boards (IRBs). Measures must be taken to ensure anonymity in such surveys.
